data.title: Design AI Prompt Playground
data.contentPreview:
## 1. What is a Prompt Playground?

A prompt playground is a web-based tool that lets users write, edit, and test text prompts against *large language models (LLMs)* in a trial-and-error loop. Unlike chatbots, a playground treats each run as a stateless one-shot request: no conversational memory, no context carry-over. The user iterates on prompt wording, model parameters, and examples until the output quality is satisfactory, then saves or exports the winning prompt.

## 2. Requirements

A prompt playground is a workbench for iterative prompt engineering: users write a prompt, run it against a large language model (LLM), inspect the output, tweak wording or parameters, and repeat. The core tension is that the playground must feel instant despite slow external LLM calls, and every iteration must be durably versioned so users can freely experiment without fear of losing a good prompt.

### Clarifying Questions

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"Is this a single-user workbench where each user works privately, or do multiple users need to collaborate on the same prompt project in real time?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"Single user only. Each project belongs to one owner. No real-time collaboration for now."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
Single-user ownership removes collaboration and conflict-resolution from scope. The versioning model only needs to support one writer per project.
:::
::::

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"How large can a prompt be? Are there practical upper limits the system needs to handle gracefully?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"Prompts can reach 100,000 tokens. A few-shot prompt with many examples can be several hundred kilobytes of text. The system must handle these without crashing, even if it degrades gracefully for very large payloads."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
Very large prompt bodies have to be treated differently from ordinary project metadata. The storage design should keep large text payloads from slowing down common listing and version-browsing reads.
:::
::::

::::qa-item
:::you[You]
"Should version history be a linear chain where every submission adds a new version at the head, or do users need to branch and maintain multiple parallel lines of iteration?"
:::
:::interviewer[Interviewer]
"Linear chain. One active version at a time per project. When a user reverts to an older version, that becomes a new version at the head. We do not destroy history."
:::
:::takeaway[Takeaway]
This makes version history an append-only timeline rather than a branching tree. Revert should preserve history instead of rewriting it.
:::
::::
